1415.title: The creed, reviewed
1415.howItsDone: Muslims learn the articles of faith from the hadith of Jibril and the Qur'an, and teachers explain each one; theological schools reason about them in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the schools, Malik's answer to the caliph, and many schools in one row. Your line was many schools, one row.

Facing east or facing west, says a verse in surah al-Baqarah, is not what righteousness is. Then it says what is, in paraphrase: believing in Allah and the Last Day, the angels, the scripture and the prophets, and giving wealth, out of love, to relatives, orphans, the needy and the traveler. A creed and a kindness in one breath, neither left waiting for the other. This year the creed came most often from a different scene: a stranger who walks in and asks questions. Today, six articles of faith.
screen: `NOT EAST, NOT WEST.` → `A CREED AND A KINDNESS.` → `SIX ARTICLES OF FAITH.`

segments.voice: In the hadith of Jibril in Sahih Muslim, a stranger in white sits knee to knee with the Prophet, peace be upon him, and asks: what is faith? The answer, in paraphrase: to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and to believe in the decree, its good and its bad. Six. The Qur'an says something close about the believers: "Each one believeth in Allah and His angels and His scriptures and His messengers." What do the six share? Each reaches past what the eye can check. Nobody at that gathering could point to an angel, open the Last Day, or hold the decree in a hand. The creed is a map of what lies past the eye: the One, the messengers between, the books they carried, and the road ahead. Theologians reasoned about these six, and not all the same way. The Ash'ari and Maturidi schools defended the creed with arguments. The Athari approach took the texts as they came, without asking how. Twelver Shia teaching arranges its roots of faith in its own way, naming oneness, justice, prophethood, the imamate and the return. The year described them side by side and ranked none. And the end of the scene. When the stranger leaves, the Prophet later tells Umar, in paraphrase, that it was Jibril, who came to teach them their religion. So the questions were the lesson.
screen: `ALLAH, ANGELS, BOOKS, MESSENGERS…` · `SIX THINGS PAST THE EYE.` · `REASONED IN MORE THAN ONE WAY.` · `IT WAS JIBRIL, TEACHING BY ASKING.`

segments.voice: One to a breath, let the six go by, quietly or in your head: Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree, its good and its bad. If these are your faith, you can say them as your own; if you're learning, just hear the list the way the companions heard it, from someone else's mouth. Then rest in the quiet after the sixth.
The creed. What Muslims believe, in the hadith of Jibril: Allah, His angels, books, messengers, the Last Day, and the decree. Today's word.
Your line: six to believe. A creed that was taught by being asked about. Until tomorrow.

1416.title: The heart, reviewed
1416.howItsDone: Muslims who follow the inward path read works such as al-Ghazali's Revival of the Religious Sciences, study the virtues and diseases of the heart with a teacher, and take account of themselves at the end of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the creed, six things past the eye, taught by a stranger's questions. Your line was six to believe.

At a checkup, the doctor does two things. She looks for what's working: heart rate, breath, strength. And she looks for what's wrong: a fever, a cough, a lump that shouldn't be there. Two lists on one clipboard. The middle of this year did the same with a different organ. One list was the stations, the good things a heart can grow into. The other was the diseases, the things that make a heart sick. Today, both lists, and the one sentence that holds them together.
screen: `TWO LISTS ON ONE CLIPBOARD.` → `WHAT'S WORKING, WHAT'S WRONG.` → `THE SAME CHECKUP FOR THE HEART.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet, peace be upon him, says there is a lump of flesh in the body: if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. And it is the heart. Everything the year taught about the inner life hangs on that. The stations, one by one: turning back in repentance, watchfulness, taking account of yourself before you're taken to account, not being owned by things, patience, gratitude, trust after effort, contentment, love, and the two wings of fear and hope, with sincerity of intention running through all of them. The diseases: arrogance, which a hadith in Sahih Muslim defines, in paraphrase, as rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Envy. Showing off. Anger. Greed. Backbiting. Lying. Heedlessness, the plain forgetting of Allah in the rush of the day. And despair, the closed door. Al-Ghazali's Revival, which the year opened, has one part on the things that destroy and one part on the things that save. Where it leads: the Qur'an describes a day when wealth and sons are no help, except to the one who comes to Allah with a sound heart, in paraphrase. You first met that phrase on day five hundred seventeen. That's the point of the checkup. Not a perfect score on either list, but a heart brought back, again and again, toward sound.
screen: `IF THE HEART IS SOUND, ALL IS SOUND.` · `THE STATIONS: WHAT A HEART GROWS INTO.` · `THE DISEASES: WHAT MAKES IT SICK.` · `COME WITH A SOUND HEART.`

segments.voice: If you like, place a hand on your chest and ask one question from the first list: where did I show patience, or gratitude, this week? Then one from the second, where did envy, or anger, or showing off slip in, and let a moment come without arguing with it; no verdict, no score. If you pray, turn both moments over to Allah in your own words; and if despair has settled in and won't lift, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour, or elsewhere, local emergency help.
The heart. Al-qalb, the lump of flesh the hadith says the whole body follows, checked for what it is growing and what is making it sick. Today's word.
Your line: check the heart. Two lists, one heart, brought back again and again. Go gently.

1417.title: The manners, reviewed
1417.howItsDone: Muslims learn adab from the Prophet's example in hadith: saying bismillah and eating with the right hand, greeting others, honoring guests and neighbors, and speaking well or staying silent, and teach them to children at the family table.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the heart, two lists on one clipboard, and a heart brought back toward sound. Your line was check the heart.

A boy sits at a shared platter of food in the Prophet's house. He's the stepson of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and he's hungry, and his hand is everywhere: this side of the dish, that side, wherever the best piece seems to be. The Prophet gives him three short instructions. Say the name of Allah. Eat with your right hand. Eat from what is in front of you. That's all. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the boy, Umar ibn Abi Salamah, remembers it, and says, in paraphrase, that this stayed his way of eating from then on. Today, adab in everything.
screen: `A HAND ALL OVER THE PLATTER.` → `THREE SHORT INSTRUCTIONS.` → `IT STAYED HIS WAY OF EATING.`

segments.voice: Adab, as the year defined it, is courtesy: toward Allah, toward people, and toward things. Not etiquette for show, but the shape a faith takes in small moments. It covers a lot of ground. The year walked it room by room: the adab of speech, of eating, of guests, of travel, of sleep, of learning, of the road, of the market, of parents, neighbors and children, of animals and of the earth. A single hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari holds three of them in one breath, in paraphrase: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or keep silent, let him honor his neighbor, let him honor his guest. Where does it come from? In a report in Malik's Muwatta, in paraphrase, the Prophet says he was sent to perfect good character. So adab isn't an extra laid on top of the faith; that report puts it inside the reason the message came. Back to the boy. Notice what made it stick. The instructions were small enough to keep. Nobody handed him a book of rules. He got three things he could do at the very next meal, and he kept doing them. That's how adab works across a whole life: one small courtesy, kept, until it's simply who you are at the table.
screen: `COURTESY TO ALLAH, PEOPLE, THINGS.` · `SPEECH, GUESTS, ROADS, ANIMALS…` · `SENT TO PERFECT CHARACTER.` · `SMALL ENOUGH TO KEEP.`

segments.voice: Let the year's rooms pass by slowly, speech, the table, guests, the road, parents, neighbors, animals, and stop at the one nearest to your day. Make it as small as the boy's instructions: not being kinder to everyone, but something like bismillah before lunch, letting the other driver in, or returning every greeting. Choose one, and hold it for the rest of the sit, as if tucking it in a pocket.
The manners. Adab: courtesy toward Allah, people and things, carried into the smallest moments of the day. Today's word.
Your line: courtesy. Small enough to keep at the very next meal. See you tomorrow.

1418.title: The life cycle, reviewed
1418.hook: from the adhan in the ear to the last prayer
1418.howItsDone: Muslim families mark each stage with practices drawn from hadith and local custom: the call to prayer in a newborn's ear, naming and the 'aqiqah, teaching children to pray, the nikah contract, visiting the sick, and washing, shrouding and praying the funeral prayer for the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the manners, a boy at a platter, and adab kept small. Your line was courtesy.

A grandfather leans over a newborn, hours old, and whispers the call to prayer into the baby's right ear. Allahu akbar. The baby isn't going to stand up and pray. There's no prayer after this call. Long afterward, rows of people stand in a mosque courtyard for a funeral prayer. There's no call before that prayer. Some Muslims put the two together in a saying people repeat: a life is the space between a call and its prayer. Today, the life cycle, from the adhan in the ear to the last prayer.
screen: `A CALL WHISPERED IN A NEWBORN'S EAR.` → `A PRAYER WITH NO CALL BEFORE IT.` → `A LIFE IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: A report in Abu Dawud's collection, in paraphrase, says the Prophet, peace be upon him, gave the call to prayer in the ear of his grandson Hasan when he was born. In Sahih al-Bukhari, a companion brings his newborn son to the Prophet, who names him, chews a date, and touches it to the baby's mouth. A good name, a taste of sweetness, and in some families a sacrifice shared in thanks. Then childhood. A report in Abu Dawud tells parents to have their children pray from the age of seven: learning by doing, beside the people who love them. Marriage and home: the year called the nikah a contract of mercy, with consent, witnesses, and a gift to the bride that belongs to her alone, which the Qur'an tells husbands to give, in paraphrase. Illness and death. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet tells his followers to feed the hungry, visit the sick and free the captive. A sick room is a place to go toward, not to avoid. At a loss, the Qur'an gives the words people say: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Then the funeral prayer, said standing, in rows, for someone who can no longer stand. Customs differ between cultures and schools at every step. But the shape stays: every stage has its words, and every stage has people around it.
screen: `A CALL, A NAME, A TASTE OF DATE.` · `CHILDREN LEARN BY PRAYING BESIDE YOU.` · `A CONTRACT OF MERCY.` · `VISIT THE SICK; SAY THE WORDS OF RETURN.`

segments.voice: Walk the stages slowly, one person at each, a new baby you know of, a child learning, a couple, someone sick right now, someone who has died, and give each a few breaths. If you pray, ask good for each of them in your own words; if you don't, simply hold each face in mind. And if a loss feels too heavy to carry alone, in the US call or text 988, any hour, or elsewhere, local emergency help.
The life cycle. From the call in a newborn's ear to the funeral prayer, each stage with its own words and its own people. Today's word.
Your line: every stage. From the first call to the last prayer. Rest well.

1419.title: The world, reviewed
1419.howItsDone: Muslims pray for the wider ummah in their own words, and send aid to Muslim communities hit by disaster, sometimes through their local mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the life cycle, a call in a newborn's ear and a prayer with no call before it. Your line was every stage.

"The difference of your languages and colours." That phrase sits in the Qur'an's list of Allah's signs, right beside the creation of the heavens and the earth. Languages and colors, counted as signs, like mountains and rain. Hold that next to the last stretch of this year. A circle of Sufi chanting in Senegal. A youth group studying online on a weeknight. A Shia family in a hall of mourning in a big city. A convert at her first Friday prayer. An imam in a small town who leads the prayer and then helps stack the chairs. A diverse, living ummah.
screen: `LANGUAGES AND COLORS, AS SIGNS.` → `SENEGAL, ONLINE, A FIRST FRIDAY.` → `A DIVERSE, LIVING UMMAH.`

segments.voice: The year met each group in its own words and ranked none. The Deobandi and Barelvi traditions of South Asia. The traveling preachers of the Tablighi Jamaat. The Salafi approach, which seeks to follow the earliest generations closely, and is itself diverse. Sufi orders like the Tijaniyyah and the Muridiyyah. Shia communities in Iraq, Lebanon, Iran and beyond, and the Isma'ilis with their living Imam. Converts, some of whom prefer the word reverts. Women speaking for themselves, and not all agreeing. Young people, and Muslims living as minorities. Variety isn't a problem in the text. The Qur'an says people were made into nations and tribes, in Pickthall's words, "that ye may know one another." Not that they may be identical: that they may meet and learn each other. What holds it together? In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet, peace be upon him, says the believers in their mercy and love for one another are like one body: when one part aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever. Not one uniform. One body, with many parts that feel each other's pain. And on an ordinary day, a body knows about its far limbs. A Muslim in Ohio hearing about a flood in Bangladesh, or a mosque fire in a town she'll never visit, is being asked by that hadith to feel it. The ummah is less a map than a nervous system.
screen: `MANY WAYS, EACH IN ITS OWN WORDS.` · `THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.` · `LIKE ONE BODY.` · `LESS A MAP THAN A NERVOUS SYSTEM.`

segments.voice: Travel slowly, one breath per place: a mosque near you, a city in West Africa, a town in South Asia, a village in Indonesia, a family in a refugee camp, a student far from home, a convert praying alone in a small apartment. If you pray, ask good for them in your own words; if you don't, simply let each place be real for a breath, full of people waking, working and praying.
The world. The ummah, the worldwide community of Muslims, many languages and colors, one body in the hadith's picture. Today's word.
Your line: everywhere. When one part aches, the whole body feels it too. Until tomorrow.

1420.title: What surprised you
1420.hook: the thing you didn't expect to learn
1420.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Musa and al-Khidr in Surat al-Kahf, which some recite on Fridays, and teachers use it to speak about humility in learning and the limits of what a person can see.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the world, languages and colors as signs, and one body. Your line was everywhere.

A boat pulls away from the shore with two travelers aboard. Once they're on board, one of them sets to work knocking a hole in its side. The other is Musa, a prophet, and he can't believe what he's seeing. In Surat al-Kahf he set out on this journey to learn, and promised his teacher, a servant of Allah given knowledge from Allah's own presence, that he would be patient. He lasts until the boat. You met this pair on day four hundred sixty-eight. Today, after a year of learning, the thing you didn't expect.
screen: `A HOLE IN THE BOAT.` → `A PROPHET WHO PROMISED PATIENCE.` → `WHAT YOU DIDN'T EXPECT.`

segments.voice: In the Qur'an's telling, the boat is only the beginning. Musa protests. Then comes a second act, far harder, and Musa cries out against it. Then, in a town that refused them food, the man rebuilds a falling wall for nothing, and Musa says he could at least have taken pay. Each time the man reminds him, in paraphrase: did I not say you could not be patient with me? Then the explanations. The boat belonged to poor people, and a king was seizing every boat by force; a damaged one would be passed by. Under the wall lay a treasure belonging to two orphan boys whose father had been righteous, kept safe until they were grown. What looked wrong was something Musa didn't yet know. Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari name the man al-Khidr; the Qur'an simply calls him one of Allah's servants. Musa was a prophet, and he still had more to learn, and the learning arrived as surprise. The Qur'an elsewhere gives the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, a line to say: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Surprise can be what that request looks like when it's answered. And your own year? Maybe it was that hadith scholars tested the words as well as the chain. Or that, in Sahih al-Bukhari, Allah divided mercy into a hundred parts and sent down only one. Or that people of different schools stand in one row and no one corrects anyone. Or something else entirely, that didn't go the way you expected.
screen: `A BOAT, A SECOND ACT, A WALL.` · `WHAT LOOKED WRONG WAS NOT YET KNOWN.` · `INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.` · `WHAT DID THIS YEAR SURPRISE?`

segments.voice: Let the year go by slowly, like pages turning: the pillars, the reports, the schools, the creed, the heart, the manners, the life cycle, the world. Somewhere in there one thing may catch, a moment of wait, really? Not the most impressive one, the one that actually caught: hold it for the rest of the sit, and find the one sentence that says it.

1421.title: What changed in practice
1421.howItsDone: Muslim teachers encourage small, regular acts over occasional big ones, such as a fixed daily portion of Qur'an, a set extra prayer, or a regular charity, citing the hadith that the most beloved deeds are the most constant, even if small.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what surprised you, Musa, a boat and a wall. Your line was surprised.

Good, or silent. Tie it, trust Him. Count before you are counted. The right hand, the name. Plant it anyway. Start next door. All year the lessons have ended with a short line and one small thing to try. A line like that can be said once and drift off with the day. That's how lines work. But maybe one didn't. Maybe a bismillah before meals is still there. Maybe a pause before speaking, or a coin set aside each week, or a quick check of the heart before sleep. Today, the habit that stuck.
screen: `GOOD, OR SILENT. TIE IT, TRUST HIM.` → `A LINE CAN DRIFT OFF.` → `ONE MAY HAVE STUCK.`

segments.voice: A hadith the year met at the charity jar: in Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha reports, in paraphrase, that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was asked which deeds are most beloved to Allah, and he said: the most constant of them, even if they are small. Not the biggest. Not the most dramatic. The ones that keep going. How he lived it: asked whether he set aside special days for extra worship, Aisha answered, in paraphrase, that his deeds were constant, like steady rain, and that none of them could do what he did. Why small and constant? The year kept circling back to it. The boy at the platter got three short instructions and kept them for life. The Muwatta's line on character, the hadith on the heart, the tied camel: all practices for an ordinary Tuesday, not a once-a-year push. The habits the year asked for were small enough to survive a bad day. And if nothing stuck? The hadith doesn't ask for a list. It asks for one thing, kept. And the Qur'an tells those who have wronged themselves, in paraphrase, not to despair of Allah's mercy. Muslims call coming back tawbah, one of the stations the year studied: turning, and beginning again. So whatever stuck, or didn't, tomorrow's question is the same. What is one small thing, and will it still be there when the day is hard?
screen: `THE MOST CONSTANT, EVEN IF SMALL.` · `HIS DEEDS WERE LIKE STEADY RAIN.` · `SMALL ENOUGH TO SURVIVE A BAD DAY.` · `IF NOTHING STUCK, BEGIN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Look back over the year for one habit still with you, however small, and be glad of it; if you don't find one, choose one now from the year's lines, small enough to keep. Picture the exact moment it will happen tomorrow, the kettle, the doorway, the first bite, the last light, and see yourself doing it there. If a heavier kind of despair comes and stays, please don't carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, any hour, or elsewhere, local emergency help.
What changed in practice. The one habit from the year that kept going, small and constant, the kind the hadith calls most beloved. Today's word.
Your line: it stuck. Small and constant, the way steady rain keeps falling. See you tomorrow.
